item.title: Damon Wilson’s Remarks at Beyond the Taliban: Five Years...
item.description:
On August 25, 2026, NED President and CEO Damon Wilson delivered remarks at the Endowment’s “Beyond the Taliban: Five Years of Afghan Resilience and Resistance” event, highlighting the courage and determination of Afghanistan’s pro-democracy movement to shape a freer future for their country five years after the Taliban’s return to power.

****

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the National Endowment for Democracy.

Thank you for joining us for Beyond the Taliban: Five Years of Afghan Resilience and Resistance.

And let me especially welcome the remarkable group of Afghans, diplomats, journalists, advocates, and longtime friends of Afghanistan who are with us today. We are honored to have former U.S. Ambassadors Ryan Crocker, Ronald Neumann, and John Bass; former Afghan Ambassador Adela Raz; former Under Secretary Uzra Zeya; Ambassador Melanne Verveer; Fawzia Koofi; Nick Schifrin; Annie Pforzheimer; and, most importantly, so many Afghan civic leaders and partners whose work is the reason we are here.

Five years after the Taliban returned to power, much of the world’s conversation about Afghanistan is still about the Taliban—their repression, their policies, and their efforts to consolidate authoritarian rule. Those realities matter. But if our understanding of Afghanistan begins and ends with the Taliban, we are missing much of the story.

Because the Taliban are not Afghanistan. There is another story unfolding—one of Afghans continuing to report, teach, organize, advocate, research, and defend fundamental freedoms; of women refusing to disappear from their country’s public life; of independent journalists getting credible information to people inside the country; and of civic and political leaders working across communities and borders to preserve the possibility of a different future.

I saw a powerful reminder of that just on Sunday when I visited the studios of Amu TV. I watched Jan-e Gap—“Heartbeat of Afghanistan”—a live call-in program. In the span of that program, nearly 3,000 Afghans from across the country called in—simply for the opportunity to participate, to ask questions, exchange ideas, and have their voices heard.

It was an extraordinary reminder. The Taliban may control the state. But they do not control what Afghans think, what they aspire to, or the future they imagine for their country.

NED has had the privilege of standing with Afghans seeking a freer future since 1984—more than forty years. So we have endured through dark times, giving oxygen to the light.

Over that time, through NED’s direct grants and the work of our four Core Institutes, we have invested approximately $82 million through nearly 600 projects supporting more than 100 Afghan organizations. Those investments helped Afghans build a broad democratic ecosystem—independent media and civil society, policy research and education, women and youth leaders, and civic networks across the country.

The collapse of the Republic in 2021 dismantled much of the institutional and political environment in which these people worked. But it did not erase the people. It did not erase their experience, their relationships, their knowledge, or the networks they had built.

And so our work changed.

Since 2021, NED’s focus has shifted from helping expand democratic space to helping preserve democratic actors, networks, and independent voices; support their efforts to contest the consolidation of authoritarian rule; and advance the prospects for a future democratic Afghanistan.

Today, NED is investing approximately $2.5 million through 24 active grants supporting this work. Those investments center on three mutually reinforcing priorities: ensuring Afghans have access to independent media and credible information; defending human rights, particularly the rights of women and marginalized communities; and strengthening coordination and leadership among Afghan democratic actors.

That last piece is especially important. Afghanistan’s democratic and political forces will be strongest when they can overcome old divisions and build a credible, inclusive alternative around a shared national vision—a vision in which Afghans of different backgrounds can see themselves and their future.

None of us should pretend this is easy. Afghanistan today represents the world’s most severe crisis for the rights of women and girls. International attention has diminished. And after the experience of the past two decades, Americans should approach questions about Afghanistan’s political future with humility.

But humility cannot become indifference.

There is a fundamental difference between outsiders trying to determine Afghanistan’s future and standing with Afghans determined to shape their own.

NED remains committed because Afghanistan’s democratic story did not end in August 2021. The next chapter will ultimately be written by Afghans themselves.

Our responsibility is to help ensure that the people, knowledge, networks, independent voices, and democratic ideas developed over decades are not lost—and that when opportunities for democratic change emerge, Afghans have the strength and capacity to seize them.

That is why we are here today. Not simply to mark five years since the Taliban takeover, or to litigate the past, but to look beyond the Taliban—to the Afghans resisting repression, preserving pluralism, sustaining independent voices, and keeping alive the possibility of a freer, democratic future for their country. And to ask what we can do to ensure they do not stand alone.

It is now my privilege to introduce two people whose service has intersected with my own at very different moments—and whose commitment to Afghanistan and its people I have had the privilege to witness firsthand.

First is Ambassador Ryan Crocker, who has served our country in some of its most consequential and difficult diplomatic assignments, including as Ambassador to Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Syria, Kuwait, and Lebanon.

I had the privilege of watching Amb Crocker in action in Baghdad when I served at the U.S. Embassy in Iraq. I saw firsthand the extraordinary combination of judgment, courage, persistence, and respect for the people of the region that has defined his service.

Ryan understands perhaps better than most that America’s engagement in places like Afghanistan is ultimately about people—about relationships and trust built over years, and about the consequences when those relationships are tested.

In addition to serving six times as a U.S. ambassador, today he serves on the bipartisan Afghanistan War Commission, chairs the Middle East Broadcasting Networks, and remains one of America’s most respected diplomatic voices on Afghanistan and the region.

Please join me in welcoming Ambassador Crocker.

Our second kickoff speaker is Uzra Zeya, President and CEO of Human Rights First. Uzra assumed this role following a distinguished career in American diplomacy, most recently as Under Secretary of State for Civilian Security, Democracy, and Human Rights.

But I also know Uzra from one of the most difficult moments in NED’s history. As Kabul fell in August 2021 and our Afghan partners faced immediate danger, NED made the decision to mobilize our entire institution to help them reach safety.

Uzra was our key interlocutor at the State Department—and helped secure the authorization that allowed NED to use our own funds to finance that evacuation effort.

That decision mattered enormously. It helped us move quickly when hours mattered, and ultimately contributed to our ability to help more than a thousand Afghan partners and their family members reach safety.

So for me, welcoming Amb Crocker and now Uzra today is personal. Both understand the weight of America’s relationships with Afghans. Both have made consequential decisions in moments when those relationships mattered. And both bring to today’s conversation the experience, principle, and humility this subject demands.

Please join me in welcoming Uzra Zeya.

****

item.title: NED Launches New Interactive Grants Dashboard
item.description:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The National Endowment for Democracy (NED) has launched a new interactive dashboard that makes it easy to access information about its grantmaking across 82 countries around the world. The tool maps grants made by NED in 2025 and allows users to explore them by country, region, and thematic focus, among other categories.

Encompassing more than 1,500 projects, the dashboard highlights NED’s support to local organizations advancing democracy in their own countries through its direct grants and grants awarded to its Core Institutes: the International Republican Institute, the National Democratic Institute, the Center for International Private Enterprise, and the Solidarity Center. The dashboard enables users to see how NED’s investments support key democratic priorities, such as countering foreign authoritarian influence, protecting freedom of expression, and combating corruption.

“Transparency is a cornerstone of the programs we support around the world, and it is equally fundamental to how we steward public resources at home,” said NED President and CEO Damon Wilson. “This dashboard reflects our commitment to transparency, giving the American people, Congress, and others a clear view of what we’re supporting and where we’re investing our resources.”

The dashboard is part of NED’s efforts to make important information about grantmaking transparent and accessible. NED also maintains a comprehensive public listing of all active grants to reflect its current portfolio of programs and partners.

The dashboard and active grant listing are available on NED’s grantmaking webpage. Additional information about NED’s programmatic priorities is available in its 2025 Annual Report.

item.title: Free Speech Is the First Freedom
item.description:
Tyrants fear free speech. In North Korea, something as simple as watching a foreign film, listening to K-pop, or sharing a flash drive loaded with news from the outside world can lead to years of hard labor in a prison camp.

They fear it for a simple reason: truth breaks monopolies of power. Once people can hear something other than the state’s version of reality, fear begins to loosen its grip, people begin to think for themselves, and the possibility of a different future begins to emerge.

Free speech is one liberty among many, and the liberty that helps safeguard the rest.

Freedom of assembly depends on the ability to call people together and organize. Free elections depend on citizens being able to hear competing ideas and judge those who seek power. The right to petition government requires the ability to criticize authority without reprisal. Even religious liberty depends on the freedom to speak, teach, and practice one’s beliefs openly.

A free society, in turn, depends on citizens being able to speak, write, worship, question, organize, create, and exchange ideas without fear. It depends, too, on access to information that allows citizens to think critically and participate meaningfully in public life.

This conviction sits at the heart of the American experiment. Long before the First Amendment was ratified, colonial Americans had direct experience with political speech as a tool of self-government: pamphlets, sermons, newspapers, petitions, and town meetings were central to the movement for independence. James Madison, in helping shape the First Amendment, gave constitutional form to that tradition—recognizing that a free people must be able to speak freely.

Authoritarian regimes understand the connection between speech and self-government. That is why they do not merely punish dissent after it appears; they try to prevent citizens from accessing the ideas, information, and networks that make dissent possible. This is why defending free speech is both a democratic principle and strategic necessity for a world in which free people shape the future.

Around the world, regimes including China, Russia, Iran, and Cuba suppress independent voices and seek to control public discourse. Critics are jailed. Speech is criminalized. Newsrooms are raided. Meanwhile digital platforms are censored, private communications are surveilled, and citizens are cut off from outside sources of information.

Increasingly, this repression extends across borders, as authoritarian censorship embeds itself in the technologies that shape how people access information. China’s DeepSeek illustrates this broader challenge: when AI systems developed under authoritarian controls reach global users, they can export limits on inquiry and expression far beyond the borders where those limits began. AI systems, search tools, social platforms, surveillance technologies, and digital infrastructure can all carry the assumptions and restrictions of the political environments in which they are built.

How NED Supports Free Speech Abroad

NED’s work begins from the premise that the desire for freedom, voice, truth, dignity, and self-government is human, not uniquely American. People do not need to be taught to want dignity or a voice in their own future. They already do. The question is whether they have the freedom, opportunity, and means to pursue it.

Defending free expression where it is under direct assault has been central to NED’s mission since its founding. Proposed by President Ronald Reagan and established in 1983 with bipartisan Congressional support, NED’s mandate is to support those working peacefully to defend and expand freedom in closed societies, authoritarian settings, and in places where democratic space is under pressure and fundamental rights remain contested.

As authoritarian tactics have changed, so has the democratic response. Where regimes once relied primarily on secret police and state broadcasters, they now combine legal intimidation, cyber harassment, internet shutdowns, surveillance, economic pressure, and information manipulation.

NED’s partners have adapted in turn—documenting abuses, protecting sources, reaching audiences, and keeping independent information flowing. From underground publishing in the former Eastern bloc to today’s tools to circumvent digital firewalls, NED supports many seeking to break through censorship and preserve independent space for speech and thought.

Congressman Dante Fascell, one of NED’s founding champions, captured the spirit of the mission when he said “The pen is mightier than the sword. Ideas do climb walls. And they go under walls and over walls and through walls.”

At its core, NED’s work on free speech is grounded in democratic values and bounded by clear principles:

First, NED supports those who defend the right to speak and who expose the abuses designed to silence it. That includes journalists, researchers, content creators, legal defenders, and civic groups who document arbitrary arrests, speech-based prosecutions, torture, raids on newsrooms, and forms of surveillance that make even private communication dangerous. Their work preserves evidence, informs citizens, and helps the world understand what repressive regimes are doing to their own people.  

In Nicaragua and Belarus, independent voices have continued reporting and documenting abuse despite imprisonment, exile, and intimidation. In Sudan and Ethiopia, local media and civic networks have worked to keep information flowing amid conflict, insecurity, and severe pressure.  

One principle remains constant: NED does not manufacture voices, dictate agendas, impose ideology, suppress lawful expression, or tell citizens abroad what to think or say. Nor do we support voices that advocate violence or hate.  

Second, NED helps strengthen local, independent media ecosystems. Free speech depends on institutions and channels through which speech can reach people, from small community radio stations in francophone West Africa, to digital investigative platforms in the Western Balkans, to radio stations serving rural listeners in Latin America who may have no other reliable source of local news.  

It also includes local newspapers, digital outlets, community radio, investigative platforms, newsletters, creators, podcasters, and other trusted civic voices that provide people with reliable information about their own societies. In many places, these voices are the only alternative to media controlled by the state, captured by oligarchic interests, or distorted by organized crime. NED helps such partners become more resilient, more secure, and more sustainable so they can continue serving their communities. These institutions keep public life from collapsing into silence, propaganda, or fear.  

In Venezuela, NED has supported independent democratic voices that have continued to inform the public and defend political space even amid intimidation and censorship. In Burma, civic groups and media partners have worked under brutal pressure to keep information flowing as the junta has intensified its crackdown. 

Third, NED supports efforts to break authoritarian information blockades. In closed or heavily censored environments, the problem is not only whether people are free to speak; it is whether they can access independent information at all.

That is why NED has supported in-country networks, secure communications, circumvention technologies, alternative distribution systems, mirror sites, and other tools that help people bypass censorship and communicate safely. In a world where dictators increasingly rely on digital controls to isolate their citizens from reality, this work is indispensable. The ability to obtain uncensored information is itself a form of democratic resilience in countries like China, North Korea, Cuba, and Iran. 

Fourth, NED supports innovation that helps secure the future of free expression. Authoritarian regimes are investing heavily in advanced methods of censorship, surveillance, and manipulation. In fragile democracies, independent media also often faces political and financial pressure. Democratic actors cannot afford to stand still. We support partners experimenting with new tools, formats, and security practices that help citizens communicate and reach audiences under pressure. Innovation is not only technical. It can also involve new forms of storytelling, low-bandwidth distribution, offline information-sharing, and creative ways of reaching younger or harder-to-reach audiences in repressive settings. Our efforts also help independent media develop more sustainable business models.  

These efforts are achieved through direct grantmaking and through the work of NED’s four Core Institutes, the International Republican Institute (IRI), the National Democratic Institute (NDI), the Solidarity Center, and the Center for International Private Enterprise (CIPE), which bring complementary strengths in political, labor, business, and international solidarity networks. Together, these efforts support investigative journalists, civic technologists, political reformers, and local democratic actors working to give citizens the tools they need to make informed decisions and press for accountable government. 

Why This Matters to the United States 

The defense of free expression abroad matters directly to the United States as well as to those living under censorship. Some question whether this work amounts to cultural imperialism. President Ronald addressed that argument directly when he warned that “it would be cultural condescension, or worse, to say that any people prefer dictatorship to democracy.”

There is something deeply patronizing in the claim that support for freedom abroad is merely the export of American values. It suggests that people living under censorship, repression, and one-party rule do not genuinely want the ability to speak freely, know the truth, practice their faith, organize independently, and have a say in their government. Those aspirations are not an American invention. They are human aspirations. To deny that universal striving for freedom is, in Reagan’s words, a form of cultural condescension.

The case for defending free expression abroad begins with principle: people should be free to speak, organize, and shape their own future. But free expression also helps build societies that are more accountable, stable, and resistant to authoritarian control. Free speech supports transparency, fairer markets, and a more dependable environment for American business, investment, and trade.

Closed information environments distort economies as surely as they distort politics. When speech is repressed, corruption becomes harder to expose, investor risk harder to assess, and predatory economic practices easier to conceal. Forced labor, supply chain abuses, and state-backed market manipulation can remain hidden from public view. Without independent voices, reliable information dries up, accountability weakens, and businesses are left operating in a climate of greater uncertainty, hidden risk, and tilted competition. That hurts not only local economies, but American workers, companies, and investors as well.

NED’s grantmaking helps combat authoritarianism, corruption, and other drivers of instability abroad—mitigating threats before they harden, spread, and reach the United States. Supporting freer societies overseas is not charity. Countries with stronger civic institutions and more open public discourse are better equipped to withstand pressure from authoritarian actors. They are more reliable partners for the United States and less vulnerable to domination, capture, or destabilization. It is one way America helps shape a world less hospitable to repression, extremism, and authoritarian influence.

Promoting Freedom, Stability, and Human Dignity 

Defending free speech is a democratic imperative and a strategic investment in America’s future. But before all of that, this work is human.

The desire to speak freely is not confined to one country, one class, or one political tradition. It is a deeply human aspiration. People want the freedom to ask questions, tell the truth, worship according to conscience, create culture, challenge injustice, and participate in shaping the future of their own communities. Even in the most repressive settings, citizens continue to seek voice, dignity, and self-government.

We support freedom of expression because it is a fundamental right. We support it because democratic self-government cannot function without it. We support it because societies that silence citizens become more dangerous. And we support it because, from Cuba to Hong Kong and Tanzania to Mali, courageous people continue to risk everything for the freedom to speak the truth and to hear it.

We will continue to do so in a way that is principled, nonpartisan, and faithful to our mandate. In defending free expression, we are upholding a principle James Madison helped give constitutional form: that self-government depends on the liberty of citizens to speak, publish, assemble, and demand accountability from those who govern. Free speech is not a luxury to be enjoyed after freedom is secured. It is one of the conditions that makes freedom possible in the first place.

Damon Wilson is the President and CEO of the National Endowment for Democracy (NED).
Carolyn Stewart is the Director of External Communications at NED.

NED helps such partners become more resilient, more secure, and more sustainable so they can continue serving their communities. These institutions keep public life from collapsing into silence, propaganda, or fear.  

In Venezuela, NED has supported independent democratic voices that have continued to inform the public and defend political space even amid intimidation and censorship. In Burma, civic groups and media partners have worked under brutal pressure to keep information flowing as the junta has intensified its crackdown. 

Third, NED supports efforts to break authoritarian information blockades. In closed or heavily censored environments, the problem is not only whether people are free to speak; it is whether they can access independent information at all.

That is why NED has supported in-country networks, secure communications, circumvention technologies, alternative distribution systems, mirror sites, and other tools that help people bypass censorship and communicate safely. In a world where dictators increasingly rely on digital controls to isolate their citizens from reality, this work is indispensable. The ability to obtain uncensored information is itself a form of democratic resilience in countries like China, North Korea, Cuba, and Iran. 

Fourth, NED supports innovation that helps secure the future of free expression. Authoritarian regimes are investing heavily in advanced methods of censorship, surveillance, and manipulation. In fragile democracies, independent media also often faces political and financial pressure. Democratic actors cannot afford to stand still. We support partners experimenting with new tools, formats, and security practices that help citizens communicate and reach audiences under pressure. Innovation is not only technical. It can also involve new forms of storytelling, low-bandwidth distribution, offline information-sharing, and creative ways of reaching younger or harder-to-reach audiences in repressive settings. Our efforts also help independent media develop more sustainable business models.  

These efforts are achieved through direct grantmaking and through the work of NED’s four Core Institutes, the International Republican Institute (IRI), the National Democratic Institute (NDI), the Solidarity Center, and the Center for International Private Enterprise (CIPE), which bring complementary strengths in political, labor, business, and international solidarity networks. Together, these efforts support investigative journalists, civic technologists, political reformers, and local democratic actors working to give citizens the tools they need to make informed decisions and press for accountable government. 

Why This Matters to the United States 

The defense of free expression abroad matters directly to the United States as well as to those living under censorship. Some question whether this work amounts to cultural imperialism. President Ronald addressed that argument directly when he warned that “it would be cultural condescension, or worse, to say that any people prefer dictatorship to democracy.”

There is something deeply patronizing in the claim that support for freedom abroad is merely the export of American values. It suggests that people living under censorship, repression, and one-party rule do not genuinely want the ability to speak freely, know the truth, practice their faith, organize independently, and have a say in their government. Those aspirations are not an American invention. They are human aspirations. To deny that universal striving for freedom is, in Reagan’s words, a form of cultural condescension.

The case for defending free expression abroad begins with principle: people should be free to speak, organize, and shape their own future. But free expression also helps build societies that are more accountable, stable, and resistant to authoritarian control. Free speech supports transparency, fairer markets, and a more dependable environment for American business, investment, and trade.

Closed information environments distort economies as surely as they distort politics. When speech is repressed, corruption becomes harder to expose, investor risk harder to assess, and predatory economic practices easier to conceal. Forced labor, supply chain abuses, and state-backed market manipulation can remain hidden from public view. Without independent voices, reliable information dries up, accountability weakens, and businesses are left operating in a climate of greater uncertainty, hidden risk, and tilted competition. That hurts not only local economies, but American workers, companies, and investors as well.

NED’s grantmaking helps combat authoritarianism, corruption, and other drivers of instability abroad—mitigating threats before they harden, spread, and reach the United States. Supporting freer societies overseas is not charity. Countries with stronger civic institutions and more open public discourse are better equipped to withstand pressure from authoritarian actors. They are more reliable partners for the United States and less vulnerable to domination, capture, or destabilization. It is one way America helps shape a world less hospitable to repression, extremism, and authoritarian influence.

Promoting Freedom, Stability, and Human Dignity 

Defending free speech is a democratic imperative and a strategic investment in America’s future. But before all of that, this work is human.

The desire to speak freely is not confined to one country, one class, or one political tradition. It is a deeply human aspiration. People want the freedom to ask questions, tell the truth, worship according to conscience, create culture, challenge injustice, and participate in shaping the future of their own communities. Even in the most repressive settings, citizens continue to seek voice, dignity, and self-government.

We support freedom of expression because it is a fundamental right. We support it because democratic self-government cannot function without it. We support it because societies that silence citizens become more dangerous. And we support it because, from Cuba to Hong Kong and Tanzania to Mali, courageous people continue to risk everything for the freedom to speak the truth and to hear it.

We will continue to do so in a way that is principled, nonpartisan, and faithful to our mandate. In defending free expression, we are upholding a principle James Madison helped give constitutional form: that self-government depends on the liberty of citizens to speak, publish, assemble, and demand accountability from those who govern. Free speech is not a luxury to be enjoyed after freedom is secured. It is one of the conditions that makes freedom possible in the first place.

Damon Wilson is the President and CEO of the National Endowment for Democracy (NED).
Carolyn Stewart is the Director of External Communications at NED.

item.title: Damon Wilson’s Remarks at the Citizens’ Alliance for...
item.description:
NED President and CEO Damon Wilson delivered congratulatory remarks at the Citizens’ Alliance for North Korean Human Rights’ 30th Anniversary Conference, “From One Spark to a New Generation,” on July 9, 2026, at the Korea Press Center in Jung-gu, Seoul.

****

It is a privilege to join you as we celebrate the 30th anniversary of the Citizens’ Alliance for North Korean Human Rights—NED’s first and longest-standing partner in advancing the human rights and dignity of the North Korean people. On behalf of the National Endowment for Democracy, congratulations on this remarkable milestone. 

For three decades, Citizens’ Alliance has been one of the world’s leading voices for the North Korean people. Your work has transformed not only how the international community understands North Korea, but how it responds.  

Too often, discussions about North Korea begin and end with missiles, nuclear weapons, and security concerns. Those issues matter. But they should never eclipse the lives, dignity, and fundamental rights of the nearly twenty-six million people who continue to live under one of the world’s most repressive regimes. 

When Citizens’ Alliance was founded in Seoul in 1996, few organizations were willing to place the human rights of North Koreans at the center of the international agenda. At a time when geopolitical concerns dominated the conversation, you became the first organization dedicated exclusively to advancing the rights and freedoms of the North Korean people. 

Around the same time, as news spread of the horrific man-made famine in North Korea, two members of NED’s Board urged us to begin supporting North Korean human rights. We wanted to help, but as a grant-making institution we faced one challenge: there were simply no established organizations working on the issue that we could support. Then, one day in 1996, a publication titled Life and Human Rights in North Korea arrived at our office. It came from an organization we had never heard of before: the Citizens’ Alliance for North Korean Human Rights. 

Looking back, it is remarkable how often history begins with something small—a publication arriving in the mail, a conversation, a shared conviction that something must be done. Before long, Carl Gershman, Louisa Greve, and the NED staff were working with the late Reverend Benjamin Yoon, Youngja Kim, Joanna Hosaniak, and their small team to support Citizens’ Alliance’s first international conference on North Korean human rights. 

That partnership, begun nearly thirty years ago, continues today. Like our predecessors, I along with NED Board member Victor Cha as well as staff members Lynn Lee and Jeeyoon Kim, who are with me today, now have the privilege of standing alongside this remarkable organization. It is an honor to continue that tradition. 

Reverend Yoon understood something that remains just as true today: peace and human dignity are never competing ideals. There can be no just or enduring peace on the Korean Peninsula while millions of North Koreans continue to live under one of the world’s most repressive and violent regimes. Peace must ultimately be measured not only by reduced military tensions, but by whether all Koreans can live with dignity, freedom, and hope. 

Over these three decades, your achievements have been extraordinary. You helped elevate North Korea’s human rights crisis onto the international agenda, contributed to the establishment of the UN Special Rapporteur, and helped lay the groundwork for the landmark UN Commission of Inquiry, whose findings confirmed what courageous North Koreans had long testified: that the Kim regime is responsible for crimes against humanity on a systematic scale.

The continued existence of a regime that systematically imprisons, starves, terrorizes, and denies the basic humanity of its own people should remain a scourge on the conscience of the international community. 

Nor has the challenge remained confined to the Korean Peninsula. Your recent work documenting North Korean forced labor supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine reminds us that human rights and international security are inseparable. North Korean workers are exploited abroad to sustain the regime. North Korean soldiers are being sent to fight and die in an unjust war of aggression. A regime that brutalizes its own people now exports that brutality beyond its borders. As authoritarian regimes become more coordinated in undermining freedom, those of us who stand for freedom must become more united in defending it. 

At the National Endowment for Democracy, we are proud to have stood alongside Citizens’ Alliance for more than a quarter century. Together, we have documented abuses, preserved the testimony of survivors, expanded North Koreans’ access to independent information, strengthened defector leadership, and elevated North Korean human rights on the global agenda. 

But today’s celebration is about more than one organization. It is about a community that has been built over thirty years—researchers, advocates, defectors, donors, scholars, journalists, faith leaders, and friends from around the world. Above all, it is about courageous North Koreans whose voices have transformed this movement. 

The progress we have made was never inevitable. It was built patiently through your perseverance and through the courage of countless North Koreans who risked everything to tell the truth. Today, that work remains as urgent as ever. The international environment has changed. Attention shifts. Resources fluctuate. New crises emerge. But the North Korean people’s desire for freedom, dignity, and a better future has not changed. 

Nor has the importance of South Korea’s example. South Korea’s democratic journey is one of the great democratic stories of our time. This nation knows from lived experience that democracy is neither inevitable nor irreversible. It was earned through the courage of students, workers, journalists, religious leaders, lawyers, and ordinary citizens who believed their country could be freer, more just, and more democratic. That journey has not ended. Like every democracy, Korea continues to face moments that test the strength of its constitutional institutions and the resolve of its citizens. Time and again, the Korean people have demonstrated that democracy is not merely inherited—it is renewed. 

That experience gives South Korea extraordinary credibility. Around the world, people confronting authoritarianism, corruption, propaganda, and democratic backsliding increasingly look to Korea—not only for its remarkable story, but for its ideas, its partnerships, and its example. I am especially encouraged that, across Korea, thoughtful voices are asking how this country’s extraordinary democratic experience can contribute even more to strengthening freedom, good governance, and civic resilience beyond its shores. That is a conversation worthy of Korea’s history, its growing global leadership, and its democratic legacy. South Korea’s greatest contribution to democracy is not simply the story of its own success. It is the confidence it gives others that free citizens can shape their own future. 

Perhaps that is why the work of Citizens’ Alliance has always resonated so deeply. You understood from the very beginning that the struggle for North Korean human rights is not simply about documenting repression or exposing atrocities. It is about affirming the humanity of the North Korean people and keeping alive the possibility that one day they, too, will determine their own future. 

That conviction has produced real progress. North Korea remains one of the most closed societies on earth. Yet more information gets in. More testimony gets out. More survivors speak. More governments pay attention. More young Koreans are choosing to carry this movement forward. History does not always move quickly. But it does move. And those are genuine reasons for hope. 

As we celebrate thirty years of advocacy, we should also ask what the next thirty years require of us. How do we sustain this movement? How do we adapt to new challenges?And how do we prepare a new generation to carry this work forward? 

Two summers ago in Washington, we had the privilege of hosting a remarkable group of young North Korean defectors. Among them were a rapper, a cartoonist, an entrepreneur, and other young leaders who had escaped North Korea as teenagers or young adults. Over two days, they shared deeply personal stories. One young woman read a letter to her grandparents—a letter she knew they would almost certainly never be able to read. She spoke of her love for them, knowing that freedom had required leaving behind the people she loved most. Another described discovering freedom for the first time through a smuggled South Korean drama and realizing that something as simple as choosing her own hairstyle revealed a world of possibilities she had never imagined. 

Those stories reminded us that the struggle for North Korean human rights is never abstract. It is about families separated. Dreams deferred. Human dignity denied. And the extraordinary courage to believe that a different future is possible. 

Yet what struck me most was not their loss. It was their hope. Despite everything they had endured, they spoke not with bitterness but with determination. They did not ask the world for sympathy. They asked us for solidarity. They believed that one day, as founding president Carl Gershman said at the first international conference on North Korean human rights, that “the long night will give way to the light of freedom” for the people of North Korea. 

Together, these young North Koreans drafted the Washington Declaration for the Dignity, Hope, and Freedom of North Koreans—not simply as a statement of principle, but as a commitment to carry this movement into a new generation. As I listened to them, I realized we were witnessing something extraordinary. 

There is a remarkable story unfolding across three generations. The first generation is represented by Reverend Benjamin Yoon. He lit the first spark and insisted that the North Korean people could not be forgotten. The second generation is represented by the Citizens’ Alliance and the other organizations, many who are here today, that grew from it. For thirty years, you patiently transformed that spark into an enduring movement—building institutions, documenting atrocities, mobilizing international solidarity, and ensuring that North Korean human rights became a permanent concern of the international community. 

Today we are witnessing the emergence of a third generation. Not simply survivors. Leaders. Young North Koreans who are artists, entrepreneurs, scholars, advocates, and innovators. Young people determined not only to tell the story of what they escaped, but to help shape the future of the country they still love. 

The greatest legacy of a movement is not simply what one generation accomplishes. It is what it inspires the next generation to believe is possible. That is why I leave more hopeful today than ever before. Because the future of this movement is already taking shape—in the lives, voices, and leadership of these remarkable young North Koreans. 

The young leaders who gathered in Washington concluded their Declaration with these words: 

“Through our actions, we hope these small ripples will lead to a tidal wave of change that brings human rights and freedoms to our brothers and sisters in North Korea. To all freedom fighters across the world, we call for continuous solidarity and action until the day our brothers and sisters in North Korea can also enjoy freedom and human rights.” 

Those words have stayed with me ever since. They reminded me immediately of Reverend Benjamin Yoon. He once said that the hardest part of setting a vast plain on fire was lighting the first match. Thirty years ago, Reverend Yoon and the Citizens’ Alliance lit that match. What began as a single spark became a movement that refused to let the North Korean people be forgotten. Today, that movement continues to spread. The ripples created by Reverend Yoon’s first act of courage are reaching a new generation of North Korean leaders whose voices, talents, and determination will carry this work farther than any of us can yet imagine. 

That is the true measure of this remarkable organization. Not only the reports you have written. Not only the institutions you have built. Not only the international attention you have helped generate. But the people you have inspired. The leaders you have helped form. The hope you have kept alive. 

When history looks back on this movement, I do not believe it will remember missiles or nuclear tests. It will remember the people who refused to let the humanity of the North Korean people be forgotten. It will remember those who believed that every person—no matter where they were born—is entitled to live in dignity and freedom. And it will remember that here in South Korea, a nation that earned its own democracy through extraordinary courage and perseverance, there were citizens who refused to remain silent on behalf of their brothers and sisters to the North. 

The young leaders who gathered in Washington ended their Declaration with a simple challenge that I hope all of us will carry forward: “Transform conviction into courage, courage into hope, and hope into action.” 

May that spirit continue to guide the Citizens’ Alliance. May it inspire a new generation of North Korean leaders. May it continue to inspire South Korea as it shares its remarkable democratic experience with those around the world who are still striving for freedom. And may it bring us ever closer to the day when every Korean can live in peace, dignity, and freedom. 

Congratulations once again on this extraordinary milestone. 

Thank you.

item.title: Nicola Bagwell Joins the National Endowment for Democracy...
item.description:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The National Endowment for Democracy (NED) today announced that Nicola “Nikki” Bagwell has joined the organization as Chief Financial Officer. As CFO, Bagwell will lead NED’s financial strategy, accounting operations, financial reporting, budgeting, and compliance functions, while partnering with the executive team and Board to strengthen NED’s financial management, operational effectiveness, and long-term institutional resilience. 

Bagwell brings more than two decades of experience in nonprofit finance, leadership, and public accounting. Most recently, she served as Assistant Vice President and Controller at the Brookings Institution, where she oversaw financial operations and helped align financial management with the institution’s strategic priorities.  

Prior to joining Brookings, Bagwell spent a decade at RSM, a leading accounting and consulting firm, where she led audits for tax-exempt organizations. She brings deep expertise in audit, federal compliance, and building scalable financial operations. 

 “Strong financial stewardship is essential to NED’s mission. It allows us to honor the trust placed in us by Congress, maintain accountability throughout the institution, and ensure we are positioned to support courageous democracy advocates across the world,” said Damon Wilson, President and CEO of the National Endowment for Democracy. “Bagwell brings the judgment, sector expertise, and practical knowledge of NED’s operations needed to maintain strong financial stewardship across the organization.” 

“It’s an honor to join an organization I have seen deliver meaningful results through responsible financial management.” said Bagwell. “I look forward to working with NED teams to build on this foundation at a critical moment for freedom and democracy worldwide.” 

Bagwell holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Accountancy from Towson University in Maryland and is a licensed Certified Public Accountant (CPA).

 “Strong financial stewardship is essential to NED’s mission. It allows us to honor the trust placed in us by Congress, maintain accountability throughout the institution, and ensure we are positioned to support courageous democracy advocates across the world,” said Damon Wilson, President and CEO of the National Endowment for Democracy. “Bagwell brings the judgment, sector expertise, and practical knowledge of NED’s operations needed to maintain strong financial stewardship across the organization.” 

“It’s an honor to join an organization I have seen deliver meaningful results through responsible financial management.” said Bagwell. “I look forward to working with NED teams to build on this foundation at a critical moment for freedom and democracy worldwide.” 

Bagwell holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Accountancy from Towson University in Maryland and is a licensed Certified Public Accountant (CPA).

item.title: Captive Nations Week: Honoring the Courage of Those Who...
item.description:
This Captive Nations Week, the National Endowment for Democracy (NED) honors people living under authoritarian rule around the world who continue pushing for the right to determine their own future. Created under President Ronald Reagan more than 40 years ago, NED was founded on the conviction that freedom is a universal aspiration and that those living under dictatorship should have partners in the democratic world.

President Dwight D. Eisenhower and Congress established Captive Nations Week in 1959, urging Americans to support the millions across Europe and Asia held “captive” by Soviet rule. In a statement, President Eisenhower declared that “the citizens of the United States are linked by bonds of family and principle to those who love freedom and justice on every continent,” while Congress recognized the desire for liberty as “a powerful deterrent to war and one of the best hopes for a just and lasting peace.” 

Today, billions of people remain under brutal authoritarian rule in China, Russia, Cuba, Iran, and other countries where fundamental rights are denied and independent voices are silenced. These regimes export censorship and corruption, threaten dissidents in exile, manipulate information, and help other governments adopt their tools of control.  

“Captive Nations Week has deep personal meaning for me,” said former U.S. Senator and NED Board member Mel Martínez. “I was 15 years old when I fled communist Cuba through Operation Pedro Pan. I was fortunate to find freedom in the United States, but no child should have to choose between home and liberty. Today, courageous people in Cuba and across the world continue to claim those rights at tremendous personal risk. They deserve to know that America sees them, remembers them, and believes in their cause.” 

“Our partners embody the spirit Captive Nations Week was created to honor,” said NED President and CEO Damon Wilson. “Many of them have endured great hardship to seek the liberties we cherish, and their courage reminds us that we cannot turn our backs on their cause. As America marks 250 years since its founding, their example affirms that the promise of freedom and self-government still inspires people around the world.” 

Together with the four Core Institutes—the Center for International Private Enterprise, the International Republican Institute, the National Democratic Institute, and the Solidarity Center—NED continues to support those working for freedom in some of the world’s most repressive environments as they build a freer future for themselves and their communities. 

***

NED is a private, nonprofit foundation dedicated to advancing freedom and democracy worldwide. Established in 1983 as part of President Reagan’s vision to foster an “infrastructure of democracy” with a bipartisan Congressional mandate, NED supports grassroots leaders striving for the freedom to think, speak, worship, engage politically, and support their families without fear. It mobilizes key pillars of American democracy, from political parties to business and labor, to support their counterparts abroad through the Core institutes that form the NED family: the International Republican Institute, the National Democratic Institute, the Center for International Private Enterprise, and the Solidarity Center.

item.title: Impact Report: Critical Minerals and Democratic Accountability
item.description:
The National Endowment for Democracy (NED) supports partners in key critical mineral regions who are working to strengthen transparency and accountability across the sector, from extraction to investment, trade, and public oversight. Their work comes at a pivotal moment: materials such as cobalt, copper, and lithium are essential to emerging technologies, renewable energy, and national security. Yet many of these resources are concentrated in countries where governance systems remain weak, leaving them vulnerable to capture by corrupt elites, opaque business networks, and firms backed by authoritarian governments.  

Instead of benefitting local communities, revenues often fund efforts to strengthen oppressive regimes and even criminal enterprises. At the same time, uneven competition for critical minerals has favored actors willing to deploy bribery at the expense of American companies who play by the rules, undermining U.S. economic interests. Furthermore, coercive and exploitative labor practices used by authoritarian actors to minimize production costs undercut American workers and businesses. In FY2026, NED supported partners across Africa, Latin America, and Asia working to strengthen transparency and accountability in the critical minerals sector through direct grants and programs led by NED’s Core Institutes. This includes efforts by the National Democratic Institute, the International Republican Institute, and the Center for Private International Enterprise to help civic actors and legislative bodies strengthen mining laws and improve their enforcement. 

NED Prioritizes Three Key Areas:

1. Detect Corruption and Illicit Capture: Supporting civic groups and independent journalists to investigate corruption risks, expose opaque contracts, and identify networks and tactics used to divert public resources.

2. Strengthen Oversight and Accountability: Working with civic and political actors to improve transparency and oversight for the mining sector, strengthen legal and regulatory safeguards, and increase public visibility of mining-sector governance.

3. Disrupt Illicit Financial and Governance Networks: Backing efforts to identify and challenge the systems that enable stolen assets, hidden ownership structures, and illicit critical mineral gains to move beyond public view.

How NED Support is Making a Difference 

  • Bolivia: With support from NED and the Center for International Private Enterprise, civic groups played a critical role in the cancellation of $2 billion in opaque contracts that would have transferred much of the country’s lithium reserves to firms backed by China and Russia. Through reporting that exposed these murky deals to citizens and lawmakers, democratic actors helped ensure that Bolivia’s lithium wealth would be subject to greater public scrutiny, more accountable governance, and decisions that better serve the Bolivian people. 
  • Venezuela: With NED support, an advocacy group is documenting illegal gold and critical mineral mining in southern Venezuela and exposing its role fueling regime corruption, organized crime, and armed groups. Interactive geospatial maps tracking mining expansion, detailed reporting on armed group activities, and analyses of proposed natural resources legislation have equipped advocates and policymakers with evidence to confront illicit mining in the Amazon Basin. 
  • The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC): Investigative reporting published by a NED partner exposed major oversight failures in a DRC-China venture overseeing cobalt reserves, helping spur a national audit of the country’s mining sector and a new certification process for mineral sales to Chinese firms. Another NED-backed civic group exposed questionable mining discounts benefiting Chinese companies that deprived the DRC treasury of more than $500 million in revenue, triggering a government inquiry into related mining agreements. The International Republican Institute continues to work with local actors and officials to develop stronger standards for governance of critical minerals. 
  • Zimbabwe:  A NED partner helped locals from mining communities across Zimbabwe participate in consultations on proposed mining legislation aimed at strengthening transparency, labor protections, and community safeguards. The group has also raised public awareness of the costs associated with irresponsible resource extraction by Chinese-led mining ventures in the country.  
  • Zambia:  A NED-backed media organization uncovered widespread damage to public health and land degradation linked to irresponsible critical mineral mining in Zambia, including flooding, water and air pollution, and the destruction of farmlands that provide food and income to entire communities. The reporting prompted the government to take corrective measures, strengthen accountability mechanisms in the extractive sector, and support victims in affected communities. 

As competition over critical minerals intensifies, NED partners are helping ensure that resource wealth strengthens citizens and communities rather than entrenched elites or authoritarian-backed networks that drive instability. By advancing transparency, accountability, and public oversight, their work supports U.S. interests in creating a fairer economic playing field for responsible companies while giving communities a greater voice in how their own resources are developed and used.
